Yes, pregnancy generally improves Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) symptoms for most women, though the effect is not universal. It has long been established that RA improves during pregnancy [d2], with 70–80% of women with RA experiencing improved symptoms [d1], and more than three quarters of pregnant RA patients showing improvement in the first or second trimester [d7]. However, joint symptom remission during pregnancy is not universal [d6], and more than 50% of RA patients still suffer from active disease during pregnancy, making clinical treatment necessary [d5]. The mechanism is thought to involve immunological tolerance induced by the semialogenic fetus, including thymic involution, decreased NK cell activity, and a shift from Th1 to Th2 immune responses [d4]; hormonal factors, particularly rising estrogen levels during pregnancy, are also implicated [d8, d9]. Importantly, the improvement is often temporary: approximately 90% of women with RA develop a flare within 3 months after delivery [d7], and declining estrogen and progesterone levels in the postpartum period appear to increase RA risk and severity [d9]. The NIH also notes that the disease "sometimes improves during pregnancy or flares up after pregnancy" [d3], underscoring that individual responses vary.
